stops.title: The question
stops.text: Every paper so far has been post-training quantization: calibrate, round, done. QVGen asks the opposite question. If we are willing to retrain, how low can a video diffusion transformer go? Four bits, or even three, for both weights and activations? Its answer is yes at four bits, with scores close to BF16 on VBench. For the LTX-2.3 study, this paper is less a recipe and more a boundary. It shows where the floor is, even with an enormous training budget.

stops.title: The whole idea
stops.text: Here is the story in three panels. On the left, naive four bit training has large quantization error, the gradients spike, and the video breaks. In the middle, QVGen attaches a small low-rank helper called phi next to every quantized layer. The helper soaks up the error, so training becomes calm. Meanwhile its rank is halved again and again, from 32 down to zero. On the right, what ships is a plain W four A four model, about four times smaller, with no extra cost at inference.

stops.title: Why video is hard
stops.text: Why do we need training tricks at all? The paper's theory says quantization-aware training converges better when the gradient norm stays small. Now look at these bars. Two models of the same two billion size, trained with the same four bit recipe. The video model's average gradient norm is about 1.6 times the image model's. And clips with lots of motion push it higher still. So video is intrinsically harder to train in low bits, and the rest of the paper is about bringing that gradient norm down.

stops.title: Help, then fade away
stops.text: This is the method. In panel a, a full precision teacher and the quantized student denoise the same video, and the student learns to match the teacher. Inside each student layer, the helper starts out equal to the weight's own rounding error, so from step one it corrects what quantization destroyed. Panel b removes it. An SVD splits the helper into directions, the weakest half fades smoothly to zero, gets cut, and the cycle repeats. The helper cannot stay, because it would need a second full precision matrix multiply.

stops.title: Why removal is cheap
stops.text: Why can the helper be thrown away without losing its benefit? This figure answers that. It plots the helper's singular values, strongest on the left. Notice how quickly they drop. In CogVideoX attention, most directions are already far weaker than the top one at the start, and after two thousand steps almost all of them are. The helper's useful content lives in a handful of directions. The model gradually absorbs that content into its own quantized weights, so peeling the helper away costs almost nothing.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: The results bear this out. On the small CogVideoX and Wan models, QVGen is the best training method at both four and three bits, close to the BF16 line at four bits, and the gap to the other methods widens at three. Now the caveats. On the big five and fourteen billion models, three bits collapses, even with training. And the bill is steep: about eleven H100 GPU days for Wan 1.3B, and about 182 for Wan fourteen B. Memory drops four times, but speed only improves 1.21 to 1.44 times.

stops.title: Activations are the hard part
stops.text: Let me jump back to one appendix figure, because it matters most for this project. Here the authors quantize only one side at a time. Four bit weights with sixteen bit activations, W four A sixteen, stays close to the original, with only slight blur. Sixteen bit weights with four bit activations turns both videos into pure noise. So weights tolerate aggressive rounding, and activations do not. That is strong support for exactly the weight-only compression that NNCF offers.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what goes into the thesis? Not the training itself; that is far beyond a bachelor thesis budget for a model like LTX-2.3. Take the boundary. Even with training, four bit weights and activations is the limit, so don't aim below four bit weights. Use NNCF weight-only compression, int8 or group-wise int4, with activations in FP16 or at most int8. The error-absorbing helper resembles NNCF's data-aware options like LoRA correction. Next, a study applies SVDQuant with GPTQ to Wan 2.2, bringing us back to post-training tools.
